title: Constants and auto
description: Values that must never change, letting the compiler work out a type with auto, and naming conventions.

content.value: A Value That Must Not Change

content.real: A rule written in permanent ink
content.text: Some values are decided once: starting lives, a tax rate. `const` locks the value so nothing can overwrite it.

items.title: Normal variable
items.text: A normal variable can change any time.

content.title: Changing a normal vs a const variable
content.caption: C++ catches the mistake before the program ever runs.
A `const` variable is a **constant**. Give it its value when you declare it: `const int MAX_LIVES;` alone is an error.

content.value: `const` is not mainly about speed. It states your intention, so a mistake becomes an error instead of a bug nobody notices.

parts.label: lock
parts.note: The value can never be changed after this.

content.value: Capitals are a convention, not a rule: `const int maxLives = 3;` compiles. But `TAX_RATE` tells any reader: decided once, never changed.

content.question: Which name follows the convention for a constant?
content.explain: Constants use capitals with underscores between words.

content.value: Why Not Just Write the Number?
A bare number in the middle of your code is a **magic number**: it works, but nothing says what it means.

items.title: Magic numbers
items.text: What are 0.18 and 40 supposed to be?

items.title: Named constants
items.text: Reads like a sentence. Change the rate on one line.

content.title: Magic numbers vs named constants
content.caption: Both give 630. Only one explains itself.

steps.note: A normal variable: the price could change.
A constant with a name that says what 0.18 is.
500 + 90 + 40. One side is a `double`, so the result is the double 630.0.

content.title: The named version, step by step
content.outro: When the tax rate changes, you edit one line, instead of hunting for every 0.18 in a long program.

content.value: auto: Let the Compiler Work It Out
Write `auto` instead of a type and the compiler works the type out from the starting value. This is **type deduction**.

steps.note: 3 is a whole number, so `lives` becomes an `int`.
4.5 has a decimal point, so `price` becomes a `double`.
`lives` is still an `int`. The type was fixed on line 1, so 0.9 is chopped off.

content.title: auto picks the type once
content.outro: `auto` does not mean "holds anything". It also needs a starting value, or there is nothing to work the type out from.

items.title: auto: old C text
items.text: Quoted text alone is the older C kind. No `length()`, no joining with `+`.

items.title: A real string
items.text: Write the type and you get every string feature.

content.title: auto and text: a trap
content.caption: Use `auto` when the type is obvious. For text, write `string` yourself. Module 11 shows where `auto` really earns its place.

content.question: What type does `auto ready = true;` give `ready`?
content.explain: `true` is a `bool`, so `ready` is a `bool`, fixed for good.

items.text: The standard library uses lower case with underscores: `to_string`, `static_cast`.
items.sub: Classes you design in Module 9 start with a capital.

content.caption: C++ compiles almost any name. These styles let a reader tell a constant from a variable at a glance.

items.title: Hard to read
items.text: What are n, p and t?

items.title: Reads aloud
items.text: A good name makes a comment unnecessary.

content.title: Names that say what they mean
content.caption: Short names like `i` are fine for a tiny counter (Module 5), and almost nowhere else.

practice.question: Declare a constant `PI` holding 3.14159, then use it to print the area of a circle with radius 5. The area is PI times radius times radius.
Try to change a `const` variable and read the error C++ gives you. Then comment that line out so the program runs.
Rewrite this program with two named constants so no magic numbers are left, keeping the same answer.

quiz.question: What does `const` do to a variable?
options: Deletes it when the program ends.
Locks its value, so changing it later is a compile error.
Lets it hold any type of value.
quiz.explain: `const` makes the variable a constant. You set the value where you declare it, and C++ refuses any later assignment.

quiz.question: How are constant names written in this course?
quiz.explain: Capitals with underscores mark a constant at a glance. C++ would compile other styles, but the capitals tell a reader the value never changes.

quiz.question: What is a magic number?
options: A number too large for an int.
A bare value in the code with nothing to say what it means.
A number that changes while the program runs.
quiz.explain: A `0.18` sitting in the middle of a calculation tells the reader nothing. Naming it `GST_RATE` explains it and gives you one place to change it.

quiz.question: What type does `auto speed = 4.5;` give `speed`?
options: It can hold any type at all.
quiz.explain: `auto` takes the type from the starting value. 4.5 has a decimal point, so `speed` is a `double`, fixed from then on.

quiz.question: Why is `auto name = "Amara";` a trap?
options: It is the older C kind of text, not a `string`, so `length()` and `+` do not work.
quiz.explain: Quoted text on its own is the C style type, and `auto` copies that type exactly. Write `string name = "Amara";` to get a real `string`.
